summary_html: Family agrees to a **voluntary service plan**—counseling, substance-use treatment, parenting classes—designed to correct conditions without court compulsion. Federal law prioritizes family preservation through prevention and support services.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: The Court held that DHHR kept its statutory responsibility for filing the case plan even after a private agency was made case manager, that foster parents may participate in abuse and neglect proceedings in a limited way, and that a child has a right to continued contact with those with whom he has formed a close bond when that serves his best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Voluntary or provider-delivered services do not discharge DHHR's own obligation to plan and document the family's case.
key_cases.quote: we believe that DHHR nonetheless retained its statutory responsibility with regard to the filing of a case plan with the court under West Virginia Code § 49-6-5

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of Carlita B.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held the improvement periods and family case plans afforded the mother were more than adequate, and directed that abuse and neglect cases be given the highest priority with systems developed to monitor their progress and prevent delay.
key_cases.relevance: It measures the adequacy of services offered a family before compulsion, holding the services and plans here sufficient.
key_cases.quote: Unjustified procedural delays wreak havoc on a child's development, stability and security.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming denial of post-adjudicatory and dispositional improvement periods and the termination of parental rights, the Court held that an improvement period is a carefully limited, discretionary opportunity that must be denied where granting it would jeopardize the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Voluntary participation in treatment does not compel the court to allow more time for services.
key_cases.quote: Where an improvement period would jeopardize the best interests of the child, for instance, an improvement period will not be granted

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. West Virginia Department of Human Services v. Cheryl M.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing termination of parental rights, the Court held that the mother was entitled to a meaningful improvement period absent compelling circumstances and that DHS failed to comply with W. Va. Code § 49-6D-3 by never preparing a court-approved family case plan or rendering good-faith assistance under it.
key_cases.relevance: It holds the agency to actually delivering good-faith assistance and counseling, faulting DHS for moving for total severance before any parenting help had been extended to the mother.
key_cases.quote: when an improvement period is authorized, then the court by order shall require the DHS to prepare a family case plan pursuant to W.Va.Code, 49-6D-3 (1984)
